title: US agencies name six Chinese AI firms in industrial-scale distillation advisory
subtitle: CISA, NSA, and FBI advisory AA26-251A calls out DeepSeek, Moonshot AI, Alibaba, MiniMax, StepFun, and Z.AI — and tells US providers to serve degraded models to suspect accounts without telling them.
author: AESOP AI Engine
body: The Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency, National Security Agency, and Federal Bureau of Investigation published joint advisory AA26-251A on September 8, 2026, naming DeepSeek, Alibaba, Moonshot AI, MiniMax, StepFun, and Z.AI as the operators of what the agencies describe as "aggressive, malicious, and targeted" distillation campaigns against US frontier models, running since at least late 2024. The advisory says the campaigns extracted billions of tokens across millions of exchanges from variants of Claude, GPT, Gemini, and Grok. MiniMax alone is cited for more than 13 million exchanges. The agencies say the activity is likely conducted with Chinese government awareness and that it forms "the core — not merely a supplement" of the named firms' AI development strategies.

Distillation itself is a legitimate machine-learning technique — train a smaller model against the outputs of a larger one — but the advisory draws the line at scale, intent, and terms-of-service. The behavior described is API-account farming, prompt fanouts designed to elicit restricted capabilities, and cross-account coordination to stay under per-key rate limits. What makes AA26-251A operationally novel is its recommended countermeasure: US providers are told to serve "less sophisticated 'downgraded' models" to suspect accounts and to "avoid informing" the account holders of the switch. That is a formal endorsement of silent model swapping as a national-security countermeasure, from three federal agencies, in writing.

The policy context is dense. This lands the same week Nvidia's Hugging Face acquisition closed at $12.9B, DeepSeek shipped V4.1 Flash into production, and the EU AI Act's enforcement teeth (Article 99 fines up to 7% of global turnover) went fully live on August 2. The US, the EU, and China are now each running a different playbook: the EU regulates deployment, China builds domestic capacity partly by copying, and the US is asking its private frontier labs to run a covert quality-of-service tier against named foreign accounts. Whether US providers will actually implement silent downgrades, and how they'll square that with existing customer-communication and consumer-protection obligations, is the next thing to watch.

Takeaway for learners: model provenance is becoming a legal category, not just a technical one. If you build on top of an open-weight Chinese model — or on a US API whose behavior may now be quietly conditioned on your account's threat classification — you inherit a policy exposure that did not exist a year ago. Read the terms-of-service of every model you depend on, and keep an eye on how "silently degraded" service surfaces in downstream product reliability. The advisory names six companies today; the operational precedent it sets — governments telling providers how to serve which customers — is the durable story.
